title: Newton's first law
question: Does moving need a push?
summary: An object keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction, or stays at rest, until a force changes that.
content:
## Everything stops in the end

Give a book a shove across a table and it slides for a moment, then stops. Kick a football across grass and it rolls, slows and comes to rest. Stop pedalling a bicycle and sooner or later you are standing still.

Every moving thing you have ever seen has, in the end, stopped. So it is easy to believe that motion simply runs out, the way a battery does, unless something keeps topping it up.

Slide a coin across a rug, then across a smooth floor, with the same flick. Measure how far it goes each time.
## Change the surface, not the push

Try the same shove in different places. On a carpet the book stops almost at once. On a smooth table it goes further. On ice, or on an air hockey table where a cushion of air lifts the puck, it glides on and on.

Nothing about the push changed. What changed was the surface underneath. The book does not stop because its motion runs out: it stops because something is taking its motion away. That something is friction, and air does the same thing more gently.

A cushion of air lifts the puck off the table, so there is almost no friction and it glides until it hits something.
## Take everything away

Now imagine removing the friction completely, and the air, and anything else that could touch the book. After your shove there is nothing left to slow it down, so there is no reason for it to slow down. It keeps the speed you gave it, in the direction you pushed, for ever.

That thought is the heart of the first law. Motion does not need a cause to continue. It only needs a cause to change. A force can start something, stop it, speed it up, slow it down or turn it. Left alone, a moving thing just carries on. This stubbornness is called inertia.

On the space station a pen let go in mid air drifts slowly and steadily across the cabin until it bumps into a wall.
## Forces can cancel

Things almost always have several forces on them at once. A book on a table is pulled down by gravity and pushed up by the table. A car on a motorway is pushed forward by its engine and held back by the air and the road.

What matters is the net force, all of them added up. If they cancel, the object behaves exactly as if there were no forces at all: the book stays still, the car keeps cruising at the same speed. To Newton, being still is just moving at a speed of zero.

Newton opened his book, the Principia, with this law: "Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a right line, unless it is compelled to change that state by forces impressed thereon."
## The law [[law]]

where Σ is the sum of, add everything up; F is force, a push or a pull, in newtons (N); ⟹ is which means that, the left side leads to the right side; Δ is the change in, how much something changes; v is velocity, speed in a given direction, in m/s.

If the forces on an object add up to zero, its velocity does not change. It can be zero, and the object stays still, or anything else, and the object keeps moving exactly as it is.

[[figure first]] Two people push the same box from opposite sides. Set how hard each one pushes.
predictQuestion: A box slides across perfectly smooth ice. There is no air and nobody touches it. What happens to its speed?
predictOptions: It slowly slows down and stops
It keeps exactly the same speed
lawStatement: An object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at a constant speed, unless a net force acts on it.
lawEquation: ΣF = 0 ⟹ Δv = 0
readAloud: If all the forces on an object add up to zero, then its velocity does not change.
recapPoints: Things stop because forces such as friction and air take their motion away, not because motion runs out.
With no net force, an object keeps its velocity: still stays still, and moving keeps moving in a straight line.
Forces that cancel act like no force at all.
A force is needed to change motion, not to keep it going.
exploreLine: Launched in 1977, it has been coasting ever since, with no engine pushing it.

checkQuestions.question: Why does a book slide further on ice than on a carpet, after the same push?
checkQuestions.answer: Ice takes its motion away more slowly: there is less friction. The push was the same; only the surface changed.

checkQuestions.question: A box moves at 3 m/s and no force acts on it. How fast is it moving a minute later?
checkQuestions.answer: Still 3 m/s, in the same direction. With no net force, the velocity cannot change.

checkQuestions.question: A car cruises at a steady 90 km/h. What is the net force on it?
checkQuestions.answer: Zero. The engine pushes forward, the air and the road push back, and the two cancel, so the velocity stays the same.

simulation.title: A box on a frictionless field
simulation.learningGoal: See that with zero net force the velocity does not change.
simulation.labIntro: One box, the forces you add, no friction.
simulation.modelText:
The simulation shows a box on a long, flat field. You choose how heavy the box is, where it starts, how fast it starts and which forces push on it. When you press Start, it works out step by step how the box moves and shows its position, velocity and acceleration as it goes.

There is no friction and no air, so nothing slows the box down unless you add a force that does. That is the world the first law describes, which we never see on Earth.
limits: The forces you add push for the whole run; they cannot be switched on and off part of the way through.
There is no friction at all, so a moving box never stops by itself. That is the point of the simulation, and also the biggest difference from real life.
The box is treated as a single point that slides; it cannot spin, tip over or bounce.

labTasks.title: Moving with no force
labTasks.task: Set the start velocity to 2 m/s and remove every force. Press Start and look at the faint copies the box leaves behind every second.
labTasks.hint: The start velocity is in the box's panel. Remove every row from the forces list.
labTasks.answer: The copies are evenly spaced: the box covers the same distance every second. Nothing acts on it, so its speed never changes. On perfect ice it would keep that speed for ever.

labTasks.title: Two forces that cancel
labTasks.task: Keep the start velocity of 2 m/s, then add two forces: +30 N and −30 N.
labTasks.hint: Use Add force twice, then type the two values.
labTasks.answer: Nothing changes. The two forces add up to zero, so the box moves exactly as before. A car cruising at a steady speed is the same: the engine pushes forward, the air pushes back.

labTasks.title: One force left over
labTasks.task: Now remove the −30 N force and run it again.
labTasks.hint: Compare the gaps between the faint copies, second by second.
labTasks.answer: The copies spread further apart every second: the box speeds up. A force does not keep motion going, it changes it. How much it changes it is the next stop on the line, the second law.

title: Newton's second law
question: How much does a push change the motion?
summary: The acceleration of an object is the net force on it divided by its mass: the same push speeds a light object up a lot and a heavy one only a little.
content:
## Same push, different result

Push an empty shopping trolley and it shoots forward. Push a full one just as hard and it creeps. Push a parked car and, as far as you can tell, nothing happens at all.

Your push was the same each time. What changed was how much stuff you were trying to move.

Flick an empty plastic bottle and a full one across the floor with the same finger. Which one speeds up more, and which one is harder to stop?
## Push harder

Now push the empty trolley gently, then as hard as you can. The harder push makes it speed up faster.

So two things decide how quickly something changes its motion: how hard you push it, and how much of it there is. The first law said a force is needed to change motion. The second law says how much the motion changes.

## Acceleration

How quickly the velocity changes has a name: acceleration. A car that goes from 0 to 100 km/h in 10 seconds gains about 2.8 m/s of speed every second, so its acceleration is about 2.8 m/s².

Slowing down is acceleration too, just backwards. And so is turning, because the direction of the velocity changes even if the speed does not.

One newton is the force that makes 1 kg speed up by 1 m/s every second. It is about the weight of a small apple.
## Double one thing, see the other

Experiments give a very simple rule. Double the force and the acceleration doubles. Double the mass and the acceleration halves.

That is why mass is a measure of inertia from the first law: it tells you how reluctant an object is to change its motion. A heavy object is not harder to keep moving, it is harder to change.

Newton wrote the law in words in 1687. The form used today, F = m · a, was written by Leonhard Euler about sixty years later.
## The law [[law]]

where Σ is the sum of, add all the forces up; F is force, in newtons (N); m is mass, in kilograms (kg); a is acceleration, change of velocity each second, in m/s².

The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. Turned round: a = ΣF / m, the acceleration is the net force shared out over the mass.

[[figure second]] Choose the force and the mass, and see the acceleration. ## Force against acceleration

Three boxes of 4, 8 and 16 kg get the same force. Move the force and watch where each box ends up on its line.

[[graph linked]] Acceleration against net force for boxes of 4, 8 and 16 kg.

Every line is straight and starts at zero: double the force, double the acceleration. The heavier the box, the flatter its line. Its slope is exactly 1 / m.
predictQuestion: Two boxes get exactly the same push. Box B is twice as heavy as box A. How fast does B speed up compared with A?
lawStatement: The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration.
lawEquation: ΣF = m · a
readAloud: The net force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration.
recapPoints: Acceleration is how much the velocity changes each second, in m/s².
Double the net force and the acceleration doubles.
Double the mass and the acceleration halves.
ΣF = m · a, or turned round, a = ΣF / m.
exploreLine: The Saturn V had to push about 2 900 tonnes off the ground, so it needed a force to match.

checkQuestions.question: You push the same trolley twice as hard. What happens to its acceleration?
checkQuestions.answer: It doubles. The acceleration grows in step with the net force.

checkQuestions.question: A car slows from 20 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration?
checkQuestions.answer: −2 m/s². The velocity drops by 10 m/s in 5 s. Slowing down is acceleration too, just backwards.

checkQuestions.question: A 2 kg box and an 8 kg box get the same 16 N push. What are their accelerations?
checkQuestions.answer: 8 m/s² and 2 m/s². Four times the mass gives a quarter of the acceleration.

simulation.title: Two boxes, the same force
simulation.learningGoal: Compare how the same force accelerates a light and a heavy body.
simulation.labIntro: Two boxes side by side, each with its own mass and forces.
simulation.modelText:
The simulation shows two boxes side by side on the same field, so you can compare them. Each box has its own mass, start position, start velocity and forces. Change one thing on one box, keep everything else the same, and watch how differently the two boxes move.

There is no friction, so the only forces are the ones you add.
limits: Each box's forces stay the same for the whole run.
The two boxes never touch or push each other; that is the third law.
The boxes are treated as single points that slide; they cannot spin or tip over.

labTasks.title: Same force, different mass
labTasks.task: Give both boxes one force of +20 N. Make box B twice as heavy as box A, then start both.
labTasks.hint: Each box has its own panel with its mass and its forces.
labTasks.answer: Box A speeds up twice as fast as box B. Both speed up steadily, but A pulls ahead and the gap keeps growing. Twice the mass, half the acceleration.

labTasks.title: Same mass, double the force
labTasks.task: Make the two boxes equally heavy. Give box A +40 N and box B +20 N.
labTasks.hint: Keep the masses equal and change only the forces.
labTasks.answer: Box A's acceleration is exactly twice box B's. Force and acceleration grow together, in step.

labTasks.title: A force against the motion
labTasks.task: Give box A a start velocity of 5 m/s and a single force of −10 N.
labTasks.hint: Watch the velocity value as it passes zero.
labTasks.answer: The box slows down, stops for an instant and then moves back the other way, faster and faster. The force does not care which way the box is moving: it changes the velocity by the same amount every second.

title: Newton's third law
question: If you push something, does it push you back?
summary: When one object pushes on another, the second pushes back on the first just as hard, in the opposite direction: forces always come in pairs.
content:
## Pushing back

Lean on a wall and the wall holds you up: it is pushing on you. Push off the side of a swimming pool and you glide away from it. Step off a small boat onto a jetty and the boat drifts backwards.

You cannot push on something without it pushing back on you.

Blow up a balloon, hold the end shut, then let go. The balloon pushes the air out backwards, and the air pushes the balloon forwards.
## Two forces, two objects

Every force is half of a pair. When A pushes on B, B pushes on A, equally hard and the opposite way, at the same moment.

The two forces act on different objects. That is why they never cancel each other out: one changes A's motion, the other changes B's. Forces only cancel when they act on the same object.

## Same push, different speeds

When two skaters push apart, both feel exactly the same push. But the small skater shoots away, while the big one only drifts back.

The second law explains it: the same force gives a light object a big acceleration and a heavy object a small one. Equal forces, unequal results.

## Momentum

Multiply mass by velocity and you get momentum. The two pushes are equal, opposite and last exactly as long, so the two skaters get equal and opposite momentum.

Added together, the momentum of the pair stays exactly what it was before, however the two of them push, pull or bump into each other. This is how a rocket works in empty space: it throws gas backwards, and the gas pushes it forwards.

A New York newspaper wrote that a rocket could not work in space, with nothing to push against. It printed a correction in July 1969, as Apollo 11 flew to the Moon.
## The law [[law]]

where F is force, in newtons (N); A→B is from A, on B, the force that A puts on B; B→A is from B, on A, the force that B puts back on A; − is opposite way, same size, opposite direction.

The force A puts on B is equal in size to the force B puts on A, and points the opposite way.

[[figure third]] Two boxes push each other apart. Change the push and the masses. ## The forces during a collision

Two boxes roll into each other and bounce apart. Drag the time, or press play, and watch both forces at every instant.

[[graph pair]] The two forces during a collision, worked out step by step with Velocity Verlet.

The two curves are mirror images: at every instant the forces are equal and opposite. Make one box three times heavier and the curves stay mirrored, while the speeds change very differently.
predictQuestion: A small skater and a big skater stand face to face on ice and push each other apart. Who feels the bigger push?
lawStatement: When one object pushes on another, the second pushes back just as hard, in the opposite direction.
lawEquation: FA→B = −FB→A
readAloud: The force A puts on B is just as big as the force B puts on A, and points the opposite way.
recapPoints: Forces come in pairs: A on B and B on A, equal in size and opposite in direction.
The two forces act on different objects, so they never cancel each other.
Equal forces give unequal accelerations when the masses differ.
Inside a pair, the total momentum stays the same.
exploreLine: Every rocket in the archive flies by the third law: gas pushed down, rocket pushed up.

symbols.meaning: A push or a pull. Here there are two of them, one on each object.

symbols.meaning: The small letters under F say who pushes whom: F with A→B is the force that object A puts on object B.

symbols.meaning: The two forces are the same size.

checkQuestions.question: You push a wall with 50 N. How hard does the wall push you?
checkQuestions.answer: 50 N, the opposite way. Every force has an equal and opposite partner.

checkQuestions.question: A truck hits a fly. Which one feels the bigger force?
checkQuestions.answer: Neither: the two forces are equal and opposite. The fly's tiny mass gives it an enormous acceleration.

checkQuestions.question: Two skaters stand still and push apart. What is their total momentum afterwards?
checkQuestions.answer: Zero, as it was before. Their momenta are equal and opposite.

simulation.title: Two boxes pushing apart
simulation.learningGoal: See that the push and the push back are equal, and that the total momentum is kept.
simulation.labIntro: Two boxes push apart, then bounce off the walls and each other.
simulation.modelText:
The simulation shows two boxes that start touching and push each other apart with equal and opposite forces, for as long as you choose. Walls on both sides let them bounce back, and the boxes can bounce off each other too.

As they move, the simulation shows the push on each box, their speeds, and the total momentum of the pair, so you can check that the pushes stay equal and opposite.
limits: The push between the boxes stays the same while it lasts, then stops at once.
A bounce happens in a single instant. A real collision takes a little time, as the graph above shows.
The walls never move, so when a box hits a wall the total momentum of the two boxes changes. Inside the pair it never does.

labTasks.title: Two equal boxes
labTasks.task: Give both boxes the same mass and push them apart with 12 N for half a second.
labTasks.hint: Set both masses equal, the push to 12 N and the push time to 0.5 s.
labTasks.answer: They move away from each other at the same speed, one left, one right. The total momentum stays at zero: what one box gains to the right, the other gains to the left.

labTasks.title: One box three times heavier
labTasks.task: Make box B three times heavier than box A and give the same push.
labTasks.answer: Both boxes still feel exactly the same force. Box B moves away three times slower, but it has three times the mass, so the two momenta are still equal and opposite.

labTasks.title: Watch the bounces
labTasks.task: Let the run go on and watch the total momentum each time the boxes hit each other, and each time a box hits a wall.
labTasks.hint: The total momentum is in the results panel.
labTasks.answer: When the boxes hit each other, the total momentum does not change: the third law works inside the pair. When a box hits a wall it does change, because the wall is not part of the pair and pushes on one box only.
